newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: ANALYSTS SEE SILVER LINING IN CZECH BANKING CLOUD.
newsitem.headline: ANALYSTS SEE SILVER LINING IN CZECH BANKING CLOUD.

text.p: Moves by the Czech National Bank (CNB) to clean up the troubled banking sector may cause a short-term chill on the Czech capital market, but analysts said they see the activity as a positive development overall.

On Tuesday the CNB placed Agrobanka a.s. under temporary forced administration after it experienced liquidity problems arising from the failure of Kreditni Banka Plzen a.s. and the investigation of people in the Kreditni case who are also connected to Agrobanka.

But analysts said the move is another badly-needed step in reforming the banking sector -- the CNB has now placed 12 banks under some form of supervision over the past two years, shutting many -- and should speed up overall market reforms.
"In the short-term we may see a slight chill on the market, but in the longer-term this is a positive step because regulation was necessary," said Jan Sykora of Wood and Company.
Most of the top Czech banking shares lost slight ground on the Prague Stock Exchange (PSE) in the wake of the central bank move, while Agrobanka shares lost the maximum daily limit of five percent.
The PSE on the whole was also down slightly, falling 3.2 points, or 0.56 percent, to 572.2 at its daily price fixing.

Many analsyts said that the heart of Agrobanka's problem's stem from its dealings with Motoinvest, an investment group shrouded in secrecy that stormed onto the market last year with a series of takeover battles against big institutions.

One official from Motoinvest was indicted last weeekend on criminal fraud charges for a debt swap scheme which police said led, in-part, to the failure of Kreditni Banka with losses of nearly 12 billion crowns.

"I doubt there will be much of an effect on the major banking shares. But it has been long known that Motoinvest was involved with Agrobanka and the market had been expecting some problems," said Jeff Ocenasek of Atlantik Financni Trhy.

Agrobanka is the largest wholly-private Czech bank with basic capital of some four billion crowns at the end of last year. Motoinvest has denied any responisbility for any of the problems at Kreditni or Agrobanka, where it people associated with the group hold board seats.
Analysts warned, however, that while most banking shares will come out of the current situation unscathed for the most part, many other major issues linked with Motoinvest may not be as lucky.
Savings bank Ceska Sporitelna, insurer Ceska Pojistovna and bank IPB have all been involved with, or the target of battles with Motoinvest over the last year.
"These stocks may find that rightly or wrongly, they will be hurt by the fact that Motoinvest has stakes in them, or has been rumoured to have links to them," said one broker requesting anonymity.
Another potential benefit, said Wood and Company's Sykora, may be increased pressure to create an independent market regulatory body similar to the Securities Exchange Commission (SEC) in the U.S..

The Czech capital market has long been cast by investors as being murky, where little regulation and poor enforcement of laws allow most trading to be done off-market with only a trickle of information being made public.

"It is a public secret that this market is a bit of a jungle, but now the question is how far will it go. It may help speed up the creation of a regulatory body which would be a very positive result," he said.
